target: General SWE / backend software engineering internships (big tech + strong startups), 2026-27 cycle

bullet_feedback.bullet: Precomputed popular workflows from a 270K+ row PostgreSQL table into a Redis-cached category tree to keep lookups within the database’s permission and rate limits, which became the Claude skill’s main search tool
bullet_feedback.problem: 'to keep lookups within the database’s permission and rate limits' is the bullet's 'why', but it is phrased as a constraint nobody outside the team can picture. A backend reader can't tell whether the problem was read-only/limited DB access, a query quota, or slow queries, and 'category tree' is never defined (tree of what, keyed on what).
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is one of the two clearest backend design decisions on the page (precompute + cache instead of querying a shared DB live), and a backend interviewer will open with it. Right now the reader has to guess the motivating constraint, so the decision reads as 'added Redis' rather than 'designed around a hard access limit'.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the permission/rate limit was (e.g. read-only service account, per-minute query cap) and what the category tree groups workflows by
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Lead with the constraint in plain words, then the design: state the limit first, then 'so I precomputed ... into a Redis-cached tree of workflows grouped by <X>'. Keep 'which became the Claude skill’s main search tool' as the outcome.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Built Redis caching in front of the Prisma ORM queries for Tortuga, the studio’s class scheduler with 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days, to reduce database load and latency
bullet_feedback.problem: Ends at intent: 'to reduce database load and latency' says what the cache was meant to do, not what it did. The 20,000+ visits number describes the product's traffic, not the caching work, so the only metric in the bullet is not attributable to the action.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A backend reader reads the number as the result and then realizes it isn't; that small double-take costs credibility on an otherwise solid ownership story.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether any effect of the cache was observed (hit rate, query count, page latency); if not, what was cached and how it was invalidated
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Either attach an observed effect if one exists, or swap the intent clause for the design detail (what queries were cached and the invalidation rule) so the bullet ends on an engineering choice rather than a goal.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Built an EventBridge-scheduled LLM-as-judge check for a production Amazon Bedrock classifier that rates research documents by importance to trigger fine-tuning only when its grades shift past a threshold
bullet_feedback.problem: Two graders appear (the judge and the classifier) and 'its grades shift' is ambiguous: it could mean the classifier's grades drift, or the judge's grades disagree with the classifier. 'rates research documents by importance' also floats between the two subjects.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: The interesting idea (scheduled drift check that gates expensive retraining) only lands if the reader knows what is compared to what; most readers will skim past it as 'LLM stuff'.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what is compared against the threshold (judge vs classifier agreement, or classifier score drift over time)
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Split subject and mechanism: name the classifier's job first, then 'a scheduled LLM-as-judge check that re-grades its output and triggers fine-tuning only when <X> drops past a threshold'.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Co-built a research tool that scores and aggregates topics to show Amazon Leo’s public-policy staff what’s popular, which runs in dev on AWS Fargate with GitHub Actions CI/CD and AWS CDK infrastructure-as-code ready for production
bullet_feedback.problem: Two ideas stitched by 'which': the product (topic scoring for policy staff) and the deployment status. 'runs in dev ... ready for production' is honest but reads as a contradiction on first pass, and the second half is a tech list (Fargate, GitHub Actions, CDK) with no decision attached. 'Co-built' doesn't say which part was the candidate's.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is the first bullet of the client role and sets the frame for the Kinesis and Bedrock bullets; a backend interviewer wants to know what the candidate owned (service, pipeline, infra) and gets a stack list instead.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: which piece the candidate built (scoring service, deployment/IaC, pipeline) and whether 'ready for production' means production deploy is pending
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Keep the product sentence, then state ownership plainly, e.g. '... I set up the Fargate deployment with CDK and GitHub Actions; it runs in dev pending production launch'. Cut whichever tool doesn't explain a decision.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Reduced end-to-end latency 34% for a pipeline routing 6,000+ scraped research documents to inference by replacing S3 staging hops with Kinesis streams feeding Lambda
bullet_feedback.problem: Strong bullet, but '6,000+ scraped research documents' has no time unit (total corpus vs per day/run), and the 34% has no absolute baseline, so an interviewer can't tell if this is seconds or minutes per document.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: Backend interviewers will immediately ask '34% of what, at what volume'; having the answer on the page makes this the headline cloud bullet.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether 6,000+ is a total or a rate, and the before/after latency if known
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Add the unit to the volume and, if measured, the absolute before/after; otherwise leave as is.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Rebuilt a legacy test-data workflow tool as a React and TypeScript Electron app with a visual React Flow editor and Jest-tested validation to make editing smoother, which 90% of 30+ surveyed developers preferred
bullet_feedback.problem: 'preferred' has no comparison object (over the legacy tool, presumably), and the middle is a four-item stack list (React, TypeScript, Electron, React Flow, Jest) before the reader learns why. 'to make editing smoother' is vague next to such a specific metric.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: It's the first Capital One bullet and the most frontend-heavy one; for a backend reader it pushes the stronger Redis/PostgreSQL bullet to third place in the role.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Say 'preferred over the old tool', trim the stack to what explains the change (visual editor + validated edits), and consider ordering this role's bullets with the PostgreSQL/Redis bullet first for backend targets.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Cut AI workflow generation time 65% to under 15s by splitting a Claude skill into focused sub-skills that call Python search and validation tools instead of searching open-ended
bullet_feedback.problem: 'instead of searching open-ended' is a compressed phrase nobody says aloud; the reader has to infer it means the model previously explored freely without tools.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: Minor re-read on an otherwise clear, well-quantified bullet.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Rephrase the tail in plain words, e.g. 'instead of letting one prompt search everything on its own'.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Built a pipeline that overlays AnyGrasp’s candidate grasps on camera images in Open3D to let a vision-language model pick robot grasps for a PhD-led ICLR project, and tuned its prompts to favor grasps that avoid hitting the table
bullet_feedback.problem: 'for a PhD-led ICLR project' implies a venue result without saying whether the paper is submitted, under review, or accepted; the bullet also has no outcome.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: Venue names draw a direct follow-up ('was it accepted?'); an unscoped venue reference is a small credibility risk. For a backend reader this role is low-signal anyway.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: ICLR submission status (submitted / under review / accepted)
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Scope the venue reference honestly (e.g. 'ICLR submission') or drop the venue and keep 'PhD-led project'.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Building RAG meal suggestions for the official UMD app with SentenceBERT vector search in ChromaDB to feed GPT-4o mini real scraped recipes, which internal testers rated satisfactory for 93% of meals
bullet_feedback.problem: 'to feed GPT-4o mini real scraped recipes' is word-order awkward ('real' reads oddly); the intent is grounding the model in actual recipes.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: Small read-aloud stumble; least backend-relevant TerpLabs bullet.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Rephrase as 'so GPT-4o mini suggests from real scraped recipes instead of inventing them' or similar.

page_feedback.problem: The strongest backend/cloud evidence is not what the eye hits first. The top role (AWS) has one bullet with no result, Capital One opens with a frontend Electron/React bullet, and the most database-heavy work on the page (B+ tree vs LSM-tree event log comparison, O(1) cancel design, 1.26M events/sec) sits in Projects at the bottom. The Kinesis and Redis/PostgreSQL bullets are mid-page and mid-role.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: In a 7-second skim a backend recruiter sees brands (AWS, Capital One, Amazon Leo) but the takeaway is 'full-stack + LLM tooling' rather than 'builds data paths and storage systems'. The systems-oriented profile only lands for readers who reach the bottom third.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Reorder bullets within roles so the backend one leads (PostgreSQL/Redis first at Capital One; Kinesis first at Amazon Leo). Optionally move the order book project directly under Experience's top two roles or keep it but make sure its title signals the storage-engine comparison.

page_feedback.problem: What a backend interviewer would dig into: (1) Redis tree over PostgreSQL - refresh/invalidation strategy and what 'permission and rate limits' were; (2) Kinesis vs S3 - ordering, retries, shard count, where the 34% came from; (3) B+ tree vs LSM - why LSM lost on reads at 2M records, compaction settings, write throughput side of the tradeoff; (4) the one mismatched fill out of 99,123; (5) the AWS capacity bounds - what is backtested against. Most of these are answerable from the page's framing, but (1) and the Tortuga cache have no stated mechanism or result to anchor the conversation.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: Bullets that already state their constraint and tradeoff let the candidate steer the interview toward strengths; bullets that end at intent invite the 'what did it actually change?' question.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Make sure each backend bullet names its constraint or tradeoff in plain words (see bullet feedback); no new metrics needed.

page_feedback.problem: No bullet shows designing or owning an API surface, schema, or service boundary, although 'REST APIs' leads the Backend & Full-Stack skills line; the backend work shown is caching, streaming, and storage internals.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: General backend interviewers commonly probe API/schema design; the skills claim is unsupported in the bullets, which a careful reader notices.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: If any existing bullet involved defining an API or schema (e.g. the Amazon Leo tool or Tortuga), say so in that bullet's wording; otherwise leave 'REST APIs' in skills but don't rely on it.

page_feedback.problem: Projects header line 'IEX Order Book & Matching Engine | C++17, STL, POSIX, Linux perf' omits that the project also builds and benchmarks two storage engines; a backend reader scanning titles won't expect database work there.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: The B+ tree vs LSM-tree comparison is the most database-relevant evidence on the page and is easy to skip under a trading-flavored title.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Consider reordering the project's bullets or lightly retitling so the storage-engine comparison is signposted; keep the bullets themselves.

keep: Built a C++17 order book and matching engine to replay 50.9M real IEX exchange messages without ever resyncing, which agreed with the exchange on 99,122 of 99,123 fills and 100% of top-of-book prices

Implemented B+ tree and LSM-tree backends for the engine’s event log to compare them on identical 2M-record workloads, which showed the B+ tree giving 12.8x the read throughput and 22x faster range queries for 27% more disk
Designed the book as std::list FIFOs per price level inside a std::map with an order-ID hash map to make cancels O(1), which sustained 1.26M events/sec end-to-end over the full replay
Co-founded a 110+ member student product studio that has shipped 5 live products
Clean single-column layout with right-aligned dates and standard section headings; extracts in correct order for ATS
